[Registered apprenticeship in South Dakota](https://dlr.sd.gov/workforce_services/individuals/training_opportunities/apprenticeship.aspx) combines paid work with structured training and lets employers build programs around the skills their jobs actually require. AI should extend that logic into offices, professional services, health administration, finance, agriculture, manufacturing support and other knowledge-intensive work.
Start with the task map. Let AI handle routine preparation: first drafts, basic research, scheduling, standard summaries, document formatting and predictable data pulls. Then move junior employees sooner into work that develops judgment: verifying an output against source material, spotting an exception, testing a recommendation, asking a customer the clarifying question, explaining a decision and escalating the case that does not fit the template.
Next, make coaching a measured production activity. If AI saves a team 10 hours of preparation each week, assign a portion of those hours to senior review. Give experienced employees responsibility for showing new hires how they distinguish a plausible answer from a reliable one, how they recognize an unusual case and how they communicate uncertainty without freezing a decision.
Finally, add one workforce metric to every AI project: time to independent competence. Cost, hours and output still matter. They do not tell leaders whether the organization is building the next generation of people who can handle the hard cases. A company that cuts junior labor today and discovers three years later that nobody learned the work has booked a short-term saving and created a long-term capability deficit.
South Dakota’s workforce strategy already recognizes that skills grow through work, standards and employer involvement. The AI era calls for the same discipline. Automate routine preparation, then use the resulting capacity to accelerate apprenticeship. The goal should be fewer wasted hours and faster development of people who can make sound decisions on their own.
_Gleb Tsipursky, PhD, a behavioral scientist, is CEO of Disaster Avoidance Experts, and author of_ [_The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work: From Resistance to Results (Georgetown University Press, 2026)_](https://disasteravoidanceexperts.com/aibook/) _._
**_The South Dakota Standard is offered freely and is supported by our readers. We have no political or commercial sponsorship. If you'd like to help us continue our mission to advance independent political and social commentary, you can do so by clicking on the "Donate" button that's on the sidebar to your right._**

item.title: The summer of the "very stretched consumer"
item.description:
Consumer confidence is down in the dumps. We got lots of retail earnings reports this week, and they hinted at the continued K-shape of our economy, where wealthier consumers spend and buoy retailers while lower-income consumers scale back. What does this mean for retailers like Dollar General, Kohl's, Walmart, and Amazon? Then, we'll recap escalating trade tensions between the U.S. and Canada and how they could hit the automotive industry particularly hard.

item.description:

The rebound ends four straight quarters of profit declines and reverses the 55.4% collapse BYD reported just three months earlier.

item.title: Meta's landmark social media settlement
item.description:
Meta announced this week that it has agreed to pay up to $18 billion to settle a landmark trial over social media addiction. It also agreed to add stronger child-safety measures on its platforms like Instagram and Facebook. Some of the changes could include new screen time limits, disabled notifications and restrictions during school hours.


Plus, Nvidia reported strong quarterly earnings earlier this week, again. And while investors have been wary of AI spending, Wall Street seemed pleased with the results this time. And the Environmental Protection Agency is planning to eliminate a requirement that forces states to publicize and seek public feedback for new air pollution permits. Anita Ramaswamy at The Information joins Marketplace’s Meghan McCarty Carino for these stories.


Check out our YouTube page to watch more episodes of “Tech Bytes.”

item.title: “Stolen election 2020”. A historically blatant lie lives on.
item.description:
﻿A few years ago I wrote a column asking this question:

If the 2020 election was “stolen”, why has nobody been arrested? That vast conspiracy would have required hundreds if not thousands of individuals committing federal election law felonies.

Now, here we are almost six years after the election. Still no charges. No arrests. Not even any specific accusations remaining after frivolous and bizarre attempts to get help from friendly judges failed.

This was either the most secretive conspiracy in history, or…it never happened.

Yet, administration officials still appear before congress and find it impossible to say five simple words:  “Joe Biden won the election.” Office holding Republicans either repeat the lie or misdirect the question.

The penalty for saying that, apparently, is banishment from MAGA.

Instead, these men and women choose to permanently stain themselves as pathetic bootlickers with no personal or professional integrity.

This “stolen election” fallacy will join other events in our history where ideas were proven to be misguided by facts and evidence. Here are a few random examples of counterfeit history:

  • Senator Joe McCarthy convinced millions of Americans there were hundreds of Communists in government. He never made his “lists” public and did not ever identify a single communist.

  • Over 12,000 accusations of “satanic ritual abuse” were lodged during the “Satanic Panic,” starting in the 1980’s, pushed by fundamentalist Christians, therapists, law enforcement agencies, and child advocates. Not a single charge was substantiated. 

  • Also starting in the 1980’s media reports predicted a flood of mentally damaged “crack babies” would become a burden on society as they aged, and it became accepted as valid. Very small studies erroneously warned of this, but it proved to be a myth. 

  • In the news now, “trans men becoming women” are threatening college and pro women’s basketball. There is no evidence of a single “trans” player in either group. None.

  • About 120,000 USA residents of Japanese descent were interred in camps in World War 2 under the presumption they would be loyal to Japan.  Although some real spies were operating outside, forcing those everyday folks into the camps was unnecessary and counterproductive to the war effort. No Japanese spies were ever found, tried, or convicted among the more than 120,000 Japanese Americans imprisoned in U.S. internment camps during World War II.

  • “Weapons of Mass Destruction” was a mistaken justification for invading IRAQ.  Both parties and the public overwhelmingly agreed. Now we know the evidence was thin and manufactured and, of course, no WMD was ever found.

  • The “Stolen Election” of 2020 will be regarded in history as self evidently bogus just like these examples. Even as time proved them wrong, very few individuals have apologized for the damage they caused by pushing these fictions. They remain shameless.

We have over a decade of examples proving MAGA has no shame (“grab them by the p____!”), and they’ll likely not ever admit how wrong they have been.

Will we ever hear John Thune, Dusty Johnson, Mike Rounds and other elected republicans say this:  “Joe Biden won the 2020 election and we were wrong in not standing up for the truth when our leader demanded that we go along with the lie.”

No, not likely; they are too far into the tangled web.

Meanwhile, this perpetuation of counterfeit history is the platform for new claims of fraud sure to come in November. 

Mike Levsen is a former mayor of Aberdeen

The penalty for saying that, apparently, is banishment from MAGA.
Instead, these men and women choose to permanently stain themselves as pathetic bootlickers with no personal or professional integrity.
This [“stolen election” fallacy](https://www.naacpldf.org/press-release/ldf-prebunks-disproven-claims-of-stolen-2020-election-ahead-of-trumps-speech-on-elections-and-voting/) will join other events in our history where ideas were proven to be misguided by facts and evidence. Here are a few random examples of counterfeit history:
- [Senator Joe McCarthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_McCarthy) convinced millions of Americans there were hundreds of Communists in government. He never made his “lists” public and did not ever identify a single communist.
- Over 12,000 accusations of “satanic ritual abuse” were lodged during the [“Satanic Panic,”](https://www.bishop-accountability.org/2021/04/its-time-to-revisit-the-satanic-panic/) starting in the 1980’s, pushed by fundamentalist Christians, therapists, law enforcement agencies, and child advocates. Not a single charge was substantiated.
- Also starting in the 1980’s media reports predicted a flood of mentally damaged [“crack babies”](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prenatal_cocaine_exposure) would become a burden on society as they aged, and it became accepted as valid. Very small studies erroneously warned of this, but it proved to be a myth.
- In the news now, “trans men becoming women” are threatening college and pro women’s basketball. [There is no evidence](https://www.sportico.com/law/analysis/2026/wnba-trans-athlete-eligibility-legal-questions-1234941584/) of a single “trans” player in either group. None.
- About 120,000 USA residents of Japanese descent were interred in camps in World War 2 under the presumption they would be loyal to Japan. Although some real spies were operating outside, forcing those everyday folks into the camps was unnecessary and counterproductive to the war effort. [No Japanese spies](https://www.britannica.com/event/Japanese-American-internment) were ever found, tried, or convicted among the more than 120,000 Japanese Americans imprisoned in U.S. internment camps during World War II.
- “Weapons of Mass Destruction” was a mistaken justification for invading IRAQ. Both parties and the public overwhelmingly agreed. Now we know the evidence was thin and manufactured and, of course, [no WMD was ever found](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/iraq-findings-conclude-no-weapons-of-mass-destruction-existed-in-iraq).
- The “Stolen Election” of 2020 will be [regarded in history](https://campaignlegal.org/common-questions-and-answers-about-2020-election-results) as self evidently bogus just like these examples. Even as time proved them wrong, very few individuals have apologized for the damage they caused by pushing these fictions. They remain shameless.
We have over a decade of examples proving MAGA has no shame ( [“grab them by the p\_\_\_\_!”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H-GP9qo7ZVE&t=13s)), and they’ll likely not ever admit how wrong they have been.
Will we ever hear John Thune, Dusty Johnson, Mike Rounds and other elected republicans say this: “Joe Biden won the 2020 election and we were wrong in not standing up for the truth when our leader demanded that we go along with the lie.”
No, not likely; they are too far into the tangled web.
Meanwhile, this perpetuation of counterfeit history is the platform for new claims of fraud sure to come in November.
_Mike Levsen is a former mayor of Aberdeen_

item.title: Grass is always greener
item.description:
The NFL is back in a couple weeks, and so is artificial turf. Several NFL stadiums rolled out the green carpet this summer for World Cup matches, which are mandated to be played on grass. For the 92% of NFL players who prefer the real stuff, it’s proof-of-concept — and could become a players union bargaining objective come 2030. Also in this episode: Nvidia announces eye-popping long-term revenue expectations, retail inventories tick up, and we weigh a tax on robot labor.

item.title: Aptera solar EV makes up to 4.75 kWh a day, independent test shows
item.description:
Aptera’s solar electric vehicle can pull more than 4 kWh of usable energy out of the sun in a single day, and now an independent testing house has put its name on the number.

TÜV Rheinland, the 150-year-old German testing and certification firm, ran three days of on-site solar measurements at Aptera’s Carlsbad, California headquarters and confirmed the car generated 4.23 to 4.75 kWh per day, enough for roughly 42 to 47 miles of driving on sunlight alone.

item.title: Why inflation in this country is so sticky
item.description:
Inflation in July remained stubbornly elevated, the personal consumption expenditures price index showed; it was up 3.7% overall. Consumers have faced massive increases in the costs of energy, insurance, electronics, and more over recent months. What does this "stubborn" and "sticky" inflation mean for the central bank as its leaders meet this week in Jackson Hole, Wyoming? Also on the program: lessons from Chicago on trying to raise money when tax revenue crashes.

item.title: One historic LA theater's 70 mm movie makeover for "The Odyssey"
item.description:
Old school film technology is having a moment this summer. Moviegoers have traveled far and wide to see Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” in its intended IMAX 70 mm film format. But even theaters with non-IMAX 70 mm film projection are hard to come by. The Alex Theatre in Glendale, California was renovated to screen “The Odyssey” in 70 mm film.


Marketplace’s Meghan McCarty Carino spoke with Miles Williams, the theater’s artistic director, about the renovation and why old school film technology is attracting Gen Z film fans.

item.title: Data centers need more examination, not reflexive rejection
item.description:
I just got a press release that says 19 Democratic legislative candidates have taken the Data Center Accountability Pledge (D-CAP), committing themselves to taking action against data center expansion in South Dakota. You can find the signers in the link at the end of the pledge below. The letter itself was signed by Amanda Potter, running for the House of Representatives in District 9 (Sioux Falls/Hartford) and Jeff Shelton, running for the Senate in District 32 (Rapid City).

Here’s the letter:

Sioux Falls/Rapid City, SD – August 24, 2026 – A group of 19 legislative candidates from across South Dakota have formally signed the Data Center Accountability Pledge (D-CAP), committing to taking action on data center expansion in the state and pledging to protect “consumer, communities, and the environment” if elected into office.

“This pledge represents a meaningful commitment to action, not just rhetoric,” said Amanda Potter, South Dakota House of Representatives candidate from District 9 (western Sioux Falls and Hartford). “By signing it, these candidates are signaling that data centers will be one of their foremost priorities in the 2027 legislative session. Furthermore, we will make sure information about the actions we take during session is easily accessible by the average South Dakotan, not hidden away in the legislative record.”

Jeff Shelton, South Dakota Senate candidate from District 32 (north and central Rapid City), said, “Many of the candidates who have signed this pledge have spent the last several weeks knocking on doors and listening to voters in their communities. In these conversations with the neighbors and relatives we hope to represent, it’s clear that data centers aren’t wanted in South Dakota. If elected, we intend to show South Dakotans that we hear their message loud and clear. Through commitments ranging from legislation action to rejection of special interest money, we stand committed to protecting our constituents.”

Both Potter and Shelton encourage other candidates throughout the state, no matter the party, to sign the pledge and commit to voters that they will keep their best interests at the forefront. The key commitments of the pledge are:

● Day zero action: Candidates pledge to begin work on protections for South Dakotans and their communities immediately upon election, before the 2027 legislative session begins.

● Rejection of financial interests: Candidates pledge that they have rejected and will reject campaign donations or other support from groups aligned with data centers. Candidates will not support sales tax waivers or other tax incentives to promote data center construction.

● Ongoing transparency during session: Candidates will provide clear communication regarding any legislative action regarding data centers on the D-CAP website (www.dcapsd.org).

● Defense of local control: Candidates will oppose any bills that weaken local governments’ ability to regulate, pause or ban data center development in their own communities.

Read the D-CAP Pledge and review candidate signees here.

I’m neither categorically for nor against data centers, but the pledge’s commitment “to work on protections of South Dakotans and their communities immediately upon election” even before the legislative session begins in January suggests a sweeping, generalized hostility to data centers. That impression is supported by the release’s opening statement, in which the group commits itself “to taking action against data center expansion in South Dakota.” 

I have to take exception to a broadside like that. I’ve done enough examination of the data center expansion issue to know that some have succeeded and that others are nothing but a headache. There are more than 2,000 data centers in the United States. Focusing on the failures and smearing the whole concept as a result is not sound leadership.

As far as our state is concerned, we certainly should examine and debate each project that comes calling. But “taking action” against “expansion” as a starting position? No way. That gives an impression of closed-mindedness, which is a bad message to send to the rest of the world and is not exactly what we want to see in the representatives we send to Pierre. 

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.    

Photo:  public domain, wikimedia commons

The South Dakota Standard is offered freely and is supported by our readers. We have no political or commercial sponsorship. If you'd like to help us continue our mission to advance independent political and social commentary, you can do so by clicking on the "Donate" button that's on the sidebar to your right.

_John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission._

item.title: How much power does the Fed really have?

item.title: How Tesla’s solar business works in 2026 after killing Solar Roof
item.description:
Tesla’s residential solar business has been shrinking for most of a decade, ever since the company absorbed SolarCity in 2016. Now, with electricity rates climbing across the US, Tesla is trying to revive it around a new in-house solar panel and Powerwall 3 — while quietly retiring the product it was once best known for.

Earlier this month, Tesla discontinued its Solar Roof, the glass solar tile it launched in 2016. It was always a tiny piece of the business, and its end says more about where Tesla solar is going than where it’s been.

more…

item.title: Meta’s push to make their smart glasses cool
item.description:
When Meta Ray-Ban glasses were launched in 2021, they didn’t perform so well on the market. But in recent years, Meta has been partnering with fashion brands like Coperni and with pop culture figures like Kylie Jenner and Teyana Taylor, in order to expand their demographic reach.


Kylie Jenner recently launched her own model of Meta glasses, called Starfire. But the campaign didn’t go over especially well, says Carrie Battan, a contributing writer at New York Magazine. Putting a spotlight on the glasses has only increased scrutiny — with some calling them “pervert glasses”.


Marketplace’s Meghan McCarty Carino spoke with Battan about her recent piece in New York Magazine’s “The Cut”, where she tracks Meta’s push to make smart glasses cool.


More on this:


The Cursed Quest to Make Meta Glasses Cool from The Cut

item.title: Trump’s reckless trade war with Canada will hurt U.S. farmers
item.description:
Here we go again.

As if American farmers haven’t already been punished enough by President Trump’s reckless trade wars, his latest skirmish with Canada will only add to the financial strain and frustration that has bedeviled America’s ag economy since Mr. “Art of the Deal” took office.

Trump is threatening to raise tariffs on vehicles, auto parts and steel coming into the U.S. Why? Trump says it’s because Canada isn’t cooperating in ongoing negotiations. Trump is so frustrated and angry that he plans to increase tariffs on Canadian imports by as much as 50%, which will likely make goods coming from our northern neighbor prohibitively expensive for many Americans.

The impulsive Trump apparently doesn’t have the patience to negotiate with Canada’s trade representatives and has decided to scare them into submission by imposing these punitive tariffs in January.

Trump’s “let’s scare the hell out of ‘em” ploy has so far failed. It certainly hasn’t worked on the combat front in Iran, and it hasn’t done much on the trade policy front, either. He promised to reduce our country’s negative trade balance but instead the U.S. trade deficit has been as large as ever since Trump took office in 2025.  

As to the current flap, American farmers are about to get shafted by yet another trade policy flop. How? because Canadians are already retaliating against Trump’s hot-headed approach. They just imposed a sweeping series of tariffs on imported U.S. farm goods, starting on September 8.

Ag producers across the board will feel the new jump in tariffs on their Canadian sales. Aware of this, American Farm Bureau Federation Zippy Duvall told The Fence Post, “Canada has been one of the most important trading partners for U.S. agriculture since our first free trade agreement in 1989 … we are concerned … additional tariff escalations and subsequent retaliation will hurt U.S. agriculture at a time when farmers and ranchers are already struggling.” 

The livestock trade has already rendered a snap opinion. Yesterday’s sharp selloff in cattle and hog futures at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange speak for the reception that the tariff news got on the trading floor.

But it doesn’t stop at ag.

Canada’s retaliatory response to Trump’s threats will rattle everybody, not just farmers and ranchers, involved in cross-border trading. The U.S. industrial sector is also going to feel the pressure. Nobody gets out of here unscathed. Both producers and consumers live in the limbo of Trump’s uncertainty and growing ineffectiveness. We all pay the price for Trump’s  volatile temperament and chronic miscalculations.

Canadians have some reason to call Trump’s bluff on this latest round of bravado. And Americans have some reason to be sick and tired of it.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

As if American farmers haven’t [already been punished enough](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/30/trump-iowa-farmers-agriculture.html) by President Trump’s reckless trade wars, his latest [skirmish with Canada](https://www.thefencepost.com/news/us-canadian-trade-situation-worsens/) will only add to the financial strain and frustration that has bedeviled America’s ag economy since Mr. “Art of the Deal” took office.
Trump is threatening to [raise tariffs](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/watch-live-canada-announces-retaliatory-tariffs-against-the-u-s) on vehicles, auto parts and steel coming into the U.S. Why? Trump says it’s because Canada isn’t cooperating in ongoing negotiations. Trump is so frustrated and angry that he plans to increase tariffs on Canadian imports by as much as 50%, which will likely make goods coming from our northern neighbor prohibitively expensive for many Americans.
The impulsive Trump apparently doesn’t have the patience to negotiate with Canada’s trade representatives and has decided to scare them into submission by imposing these punitive tariffs in January.
Trump’s “let’s scare the hell out of ‘em” ploy has so far failed. It certainly hasn’t worked on the combat front in Iran, and it hasn’t done much on the trade policy front, either. He promised to reduce our country’s negative trade balance but instead the U.S. [trade deficit](https://tradingeconomics.com/united-states/balance-of-trade) has been as [large as ever](https://www.macrotrends.net/global-metrics/countries/usa/united-states/trade-balance-deficit) since Trump took office in 2025.
As to the current flap, American farmers are about to get shafted by yet another trade policy flop. How? because Canadians are [already retaliating](https://www.nbcnews.com/business/consumer/canada-retaliates-against-trump-tariffs-rcna594280) against Trump’s hot-headed approach. They just imposed a sweeping series of tariffs on imported U.S. farm goods, starting on September 8.
Ag producers across the board will feel the new jump in tariffs on their Canadian sales. Aware of this, American Farm Bureau Federation Zippy Duvall told [The Fence Post](https://www.thefencepost.com/news/us-canadian-trade-situation-worsens/), _“Canada has been one of the most important trading partners for U.S. agriculture since our first free trade agreement in 1989 … we are concerned … additional tariff escalations and subsequent retaliation will hurt U.S. agriculture at a time when farmers and ranchers are already struggling.”_
The livestock trade has already rendered a snap opinion. Yesterday’s sharp selloff in [cattle](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/@LC.1) and [hog](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/@FC.1) futures at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange speak for the reception that the tariff news got on the trading floor.
But it doesn’t stop at ag.
Canada’s retaliatory response to Trump’s threats [will rattle everybody](https://www.agrolatam.com/usa/news/canada-tariffs-us-agriculture-farm-exports/), not just farmers and ranchers, involved in cross-border trading. The [U.S. industrial sector](https://www.wsj.com/world/americas/canada-tariffs-us-economy-impact-ef702321) is also going to feel the pressure. Nobody gets out of here unscathed. Both [producers](https://www.jec.senate.gov/public/index.cfm/democrats/2025/8/new-report-uncertainty-from-trump-s-tariffs-derails-u-s-manufacturing-in-both-the-short-and-long-term) and [consumers](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c98qjl76eyro) live in the limbo of Trump’s uncertainty and growing [ineffectiveness](https://yougov.com/en-us/articles/54936-two-thirds-americans-think-donald-trump-ineffective-negotiations-iran-june-5-8-2026-economist-yougov-poll). We all pay the price for Trump’s [volatile temperament](https://digitalcommons.csbsju.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1109&context=psychology_pubs) and [chronic miscalculations](https://www.aol.com/articles/donald-trump-miscalculation-exposed-203541226.html).
Canadians have some reason to call Trump’s bluff on this latest round of bravado. And Americans have some reason to be sick and tired of it.
_John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. item.title: Preparing for an AI tax crisis
item.description:
If artificial intelligence really does replace human labor, the U.S. could be in for a tax revenue crisis. That’s because high unemployment shrinks the pool of taxable wages. In this episode, we visit Akron, Ohio — the former tire capital of the world — to learn what happens when lost jobs snowball into lost government funding. Plus: Economists hope for cake but will settle for crumbs in Fed Chair Warsh’s Jackson Hole Symposium speech, and a new plan for Colorado River drought management draws backlash.

item.title: I tested this lithium-ion battery charging cabinet as the safest place to charge your e-bike batteries
item.description:
One of the most common questions I get from readers isn’t just about speed or range anymore. Increasingly, I’m hearing more questions about battery safety.

People see the occasional viral video of an e-bike battery fire and wonder if they should be worried about charging their battery in the garage, apartment, or workshop. The reality is that quality lithium-ion batteries from reputable manufacturers are remarkably safe, but when failures do occur, they can be dramatic enough that many riders want an extra layer of protection.

That’s where products like Yolin’s lithium-ion battery charging cabinet come in. I recently spent some time testing the cabinet, and while I admittedly wasn’t sure what to expect going in, I came away more impressed than I anticipated.

item.title: California's data and privacy laws aren't being followed
item.description:
California promised consumers an easier way to protect their personal data. Since 2024, the Delete Act has required the state registration of data brokers — businesses that collect and sell personal data from our digital footprints — and it also mandates they give consumers a way to request their data be deleted and report how many requests they get.


But, a new Stanford report shows registered data brokers are largely ignoring the laws. Jennifer King, privacy and data policy fellow at Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered AI, says only 9% of data brokers are in compliance.


More on this:


“Regulating Data Brokers in the Age of AI: A California Case Study” from Stanford’s Institute for Human-Centered AI


“About DROP and the Delete Act” from the California Privacy Protection Agency

item.title: Stock market volatility? It’s in the eye of the beholder. Stay calm
item.description:
On the last Wednesday in July, I got several phone calls from clients. On the last Friday in July, nobody called. Why the difference? On Wednesday, the S&P 500 dropped 1.52 percent and the Nasdaq composite dropped 1.74 percent. On Friday, the S&P 500 gained 0.7 percent and the Nasdaq gained 1 percent.

Plenty happened in between those two days. The Federal Reserve held rates steady and gave no guidance about what comes next. Major international companies reported earnings; one gained 15 percent and another lost 7 percent. Oil prices moved based on the war with Iran. All these events earned headlines. None of them changed where the month ended.

For the last week of July, the S&P 500 and the Dow each finished up about 1 percent. For the month, the S&P 500 finished down 0.1 percent and the Dow finished up 0.3 percent. A volatile month ended almost exactly where it started.

How volatile your portfolio feels depends mostly on how often you look at it. Daily prices jump around. Weekly prices jump less. Monthly prices are smoother than weekly, and annual prices are smoother than monthly. Checking more frequently does not change your investment. It does change your level of anxiety.

To understand this, think of the value of your house. Most people believe home values rise steadily along with inflation, and they believe it partly because nobody appraises a house every morning. If strangers knocked on your door each day with firm cash offers, you would watch your home value fluctuate the way your 401(k) does.

Frequent checking produces fear. Losing money feels considerably worse than gaining the same amount feels good, so every look at a falling balance registers as a small emergency. The more emergencies you live through, the more likely you are to act on one. I have seen clients sell because of a sudden drop and then spend two years waiting for a re-entry point that never felt safe enough.

Since 1980 the S&P 500 has fallen an average of 14.2 percent at some point during each calendar year, according to J.P. Morgan's Guide to the Markets. Annual returns were still positive in 35 of those 46 years.

Even the worst stretch on record is milder than most people assume. The weakest ten-year run for the S&P 500 in the modern era was 2000 through 2009. It included a 22.1 percent loss in 2002 and a 36.6 percent loss in 2008, yet the decade’s annualized loss was 0.95 percent. Investors who held through the two worst years came out roughly even after ten years.

The S&P 500 spent July going nowhere. Whether that month was calm or nerve-racking depended on how often you checked your portfolio. Over the years I’ve received plenty of client calls about dramatic daily market drops. I have never had a client call about a flat month.

So my suggestion is to look less often, even if you have to start gradually. Move from daily to weekly. When weekly stops bothering you, move to monthly by reading statements when you get them instead of logging in at other times. To make it easier, turn off price alerts on your phone and take brokerage apps off your home screen. This reduces opportunities to react.

I wrote several years ago that the only thing you can count on the stock market to do is fluctuate, and that the wisest response is usually to do nothing. Nothing in the past few weeks has changed my mind. Looking less often will not change your return. It will make you far less likely to damage the return you already have.

item.title: Does Canada need new energy partners?

item.title: Tesla loses another top chip engineer to ex-Dojo startup DensityAI
item.description:
Tesla has lost another senior chip engineer to DensityAI, the AI hardware startup built out of its own former Dojo team. Shishuang Sun, who spent more than five years as a Tesla AI hardware architect on Dojo and the Autopilot computers, now lists his role as “Packaging and System Hardware” at DensityAI, starting in July.

This is not a junior loss. Sun left Tesla as Senior Director of AI Hardware Design — one of the people responsible for turning Tesla’s custom silicon into working systems, exactly the expertise Tesla needs as it stakes its valuation on in-house AI chips.

This is not a junior loss. Sun left Tesla as Senior Director of AI Hardware Design — one of the people responsible for turning Tesla’s custom silicon into working systems, exactly the expertise Tesla needs as it stakes its valuation on in-house AI chips.

item.title: Trump plan to import ground beef is more about baloney than beef
item.description:
Cattle producers are fuming at President Trump's decision last week to bring 300 metric tons of ground beef into the country, tariff free. With cattle markets falling hard since the first of August, this added supply of foreign beef sends a negative signal to ranchers.

That doesn’t seem to bother Trump, who said he’s doing it “to substantially lower the price of ground beef for working American families.”

To that I’d say his expectations are unrealistic. He’s overstating the downside pricing effect of putting this relatively piddly amount of beef into the market.

First of all, how many pounds of beef are we talking about?  300 tons is 600,000 pounds, which sounds like a lot, but is actually a fraction of total beef consumption in the United States, where people eat about 28 billion pounds (roughly 14 million tons) of beef every year. That equates to 76 million pounds a day.

I don’t get where adding 600,000 pounds of imported beef to the supply chain will have much of an impact on prices at retail outlets and I doubt that it will. Trump is putting on a show, acting like he’s doing something about inflation. Substantive results won’t materialize.

Still, he’s determined to promote his fantasy, saying that “we have a commitment that this beef will be sold at 25 percent below current market prices.”

Where those commitments come from and how they’ll be put into place is another story. I mean, where, when and how will this beef be segregated from higher priced domestic supplies, and who will be the consumers purchasing it?

More interesting though is that Trump is apparently requiring retailers to set their prices for this imported commodity. That’s a common tactic in controlled economies, and is also a classic example of how communism works, where prices are set by the authorities, not by the market. Since when does a Republican, and one who is lately using the word “communist” to describe  American Democrats, step into the market place to make sure goods are sold at a price determined by him?

That’s about as communist as it gets, isn’t it? Don’t know about you, but I can’t wait to sink my teeth into a “commie burger.” Karl Marx would approve.

In the meantime, cattle producers and their representatives in Congress are making a justified  fuss over the president’s decision. The amount may be negligible, but the precedent isn’t the most promising for the livestock industry.

Oh, and there’s one more thing.  Trump’s explanation that removing tariffs will cheapen beef is a tacit – no, a brazen – admission that despite his claims otherwise, tariffs actually do raise prices for consumers.

Trump and his misguided advisors must believe this move will give Trump some creds as an inflation fighter, but I doubt that people are buying it. This plan is more about baloney than beef.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

item.title: AI loves negative parallelism
item.description:
Anthropic recently announced it's adding watermarks to all text outputted by its chatbot Claude. But often, you don't need fancy detection software to know; you just need to look for language that gets repeated over and over by AI chatbots, like “it's not X, it's Y.”


That's a rhetorical structure referred to as negative parallelism. And it's the topic for today's “Uncanny AI,” those times when it becomes clear AI doesn't think like us. Will Oremus recently wrote about this AI tic for The Atlantic.


More on this


“The Most Famous AI Writing Tic Is Also the Most Mysterious” from The Atlantic


“Move Over Em-Dash, There’s a New AI Tell in Town” from Ai-Ai-OH

item.title: Trump’s promise goes pfft. U.S. debt, now $40 trillion, is up, not down
item.description:
This week’s announcement that our nation’s debt has surpassed $40 trillion should be received with a collective sense of disgust.

After his history of broken promises on this, there’s no point expecting President Trump to get involved. He pledged to start whittling down the debt once he took office in 2025. He made the same promise before he took office in 2016.  

Did he deliver? Please. So far he’s delivered squat. The debt increased during both of his terms. He’s hopeless. I recently discussed Trump’s inauthenticity, a quality that has been exposed — no, highlighted — by the run-up of red ink that has taken place during his time in the White House.

Trump’s lack of success at reining in our nation’s debt after he promised unequivocally to do so may well be the most significant failure of his presidency.

How’s that? I’ll let Ben Tomchik, Vice President and Deputy Chief of Staff of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget explain the implications of all this. In an email titled “Three reasons to worry about rising Treasuries,” Tomchik’s organization writes: 

Interest rates on U.S. Treasury bonds recently rose to levels not seen in decades. A recent 30-year Treasury auction ended with yields at over 5.2% – the highest at auction since 2001. Market yields rose further, reaching over 5.3% on August 17, the highest level since 2007. Analysts cite a variety of factors driving the rise, including economic fallout from the war in Iran, persistent inflation, competition for borrowing due to AI investment, and increasing federal budget deficits. The Congressional Budget Office recently raised its estimate of the FY 2026 deficit from $1.9 trillion to $2.1 trillion, with a $432 billion deficit in July alone.

Here are three reasons to worry about higher interest rates on Treasuries:

1) Higher Rates Harm Affordability

Treasury rates serve as the benchmark for borrowing throughout the economy. As Treasury rates rise, so too do the interest rates for home mortgages, auto loans, and credit cards. For example, 30-year mortgage rates recently rose to 6.7%, the highest in about a year. Rising borrowing costs discourage capital investment, harm small business formation, weaken housing affordability, and ultimately slow wage and economic growth. One of the best things policymakers could do to address affordability concerns is to reduce federal borrowing and put us on a path to achieve a 3% deficit-to-GDP target.

2) Government Interest Expense Grows Even Larger

Increased Treasury rates combined with historically high debt lead to skyrocketing interest costs for the federal government. Over $1 trillion will be spent this fiscal year on interest alone, with more than $16 trillion total projected over the coming decade. But if interest rates remain high this year and are 1 percentage point higher than projected over the next decade, it would add another $3.5 trillion to the debt. Interest is the fastest growing line item in the budget, and we’re spending more on interest than on defense or Medicaid. Every dollar spent on interest is one that cannot be used elsewhere, reducing flexibility for the government to respond to emerging threats and opportunities.

3) We Risk Entering a Debt Spiral

While no one knows when the actual debt “tipping point” will occur, one thing that becomes increasingly likely as rates rise is a potential debt spiral. This can occur when the average interest rate paid on debt is higher than the rate of economic growth. For most of the last 60 years, the interest rate has been below the economic growth rate except for brief periods of economic contraction. But since 2023, most new debt has been issued at rates above the expected long-term growth rate. Once the average interest rate on debt exceeds the growth rate, the debt-to-GDP ratio grows indefinitely – potentially leading to a fiscal crisis.

It’s clear that Trump is helpless to do anything about this. The nation’s soaring debt numbers have obliterated his promises to get our deficits under control. 

So what to do about the situation? There are many options, but we need people who can exercise them. It would be helpful if we sent representatives to Washington who take the nation’s debt obligations more seriously than those who are there now. I’m sure most sitting representatives will contend that they do take the red ink seriously … but we don’t need them and their unfulfilled rhetoric. We need elected officials who take oversized debt seriously enough to actually do something about it.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

He made the same promise before he took office in [2016](https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/fact-checker/wp/2016/04/02/trumps-nonsensical-claim-he-can-eliminate-19-trillion-in-debt-in-eight-years/).
Did he deliver? Please. So far he’s delivered squat. The debt increased during [both](https://www.crfb.org/blogs/how-much-did-president-trump-add-debt) of his [terms](https://www.jec.senate.gov/public/vendor/_accounts/JEC-R/debt/Monthly%20Debt%20Update.html). He’s hopeless. I [recently discussed](https://www.sdstandardnow.com/home/angst-authenticity-and-the-absurd-the-existential-donald-trump) Trump’s inauthenticity, a quality that has been exposed — no, highlighted — by the run-up of red ink that has taken place during his time in the White House.
Trump’s lack of success at reining in our nation’s debt after he promised unequivocally to do so may well be the most significant failure of his presidency.
How’s that? I’ll let Ben Tomchik, Vice President and Deputy Chief of Staff of the [Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget](https://www.crfb.org/) explain the implications of all this. In an email titled “Three reasons to worry about rising Treasuries,” Tomchik’s organization writes:
_Interest rates on U.S. Treasury bonds recently rose to levels not seen in decades. A recent 30-year Treasury auction ended with yields at over 5.2% – the highest at auction since 2001. Market yields rose further, reaching over 5.3% on August 17, the highest level since 2007. Analysts cite a variety of factors driving the rise, including economic fallout from the war in Iran, persistent inflation, competition for borrowing due to AI investment, and increasing federal budget deficits. The Congressional Budget Office recently raised its estimate of the FY 2026 deficit from $1.9 trillion to $2.1 trillion, with a $432 billion deficit in July alone._
_Here are three reasons to worry about higher interest rates on Treasuries:_
**_1) Higher Rates Harm Affordability_**
_Treasury rates serve as the benchmark for borrowing throughout the economy. As Treasury rates rise, so too do the interest rates for home mortgages, auto loans, and credit cards. For example, 30-year mortgage rates recently rose to 6.7%, the highest in about a year. Rising borrowing costs discourage capital investment, harm small business formation, weaken housing affordability, and ultimately slow wage and economic growth. One of the best things policymakers could do to address affordability concerns is to reduce federal borrowing and put us on a path to achieve a 3% deficit-to-GDP target._
**_2) Government Interest Expense Grows Even Larger_**
_Increased Treasury rates combined with historically high debt lead to skyrocketing interest costs for the federal government. Over $1 trillion will be spent this fiscal year on interest alone, with more than $16 trillion total projected over the coming decade. But if interest rates remain high this year and are 1 percentage point higher than projected over the next decade, it would add another $3.5 trillion to the debt. Interest is the fastest growing line item in the budget, and we’re spending more on interest than on defense or Medicaid. Every dollar spent on interest is one that cannot be used elsewhere, reducing flexibility for the government to respond to emerging threats and opportunities._
**_3) We Risk Entering a Debt Spiral_**
_While no one knows when the actual debt “tipping point” will occur, one thing that becomes increasingly likely as rates rise is a potential debt spiral. This can occur when the average interest rate paid on debt is higher than the rate of economic growth. For most of the last 60 years, the interest rate has been below the economic growth rate except for brief periods of economic contraction. But since 2023, most new debt has been issued at rates above the expected long-term growth rate. Once the average interest rate on debt exceeds the growth rate, the debt-to-GDP ratio grows indefinitely – potentially leading to a fiscal crisis._
It’s clear that Trump is helpless to do anything about this. The nation’s soaring debt numbers have obliterated his promises to get our deficits under control.
So what to do about the situation? There are [many options](https://www.pgpf.org/article/76-options-for-reducing-the-deficit/), but we need people who can exercise them. It would be helpful if we sent representatives to Washington who take the nation’s debt obligations more seriously than those who are there now. I’m sure most sitting representatives will contend that they do take the red ink seriously … but we don’t need them and their unfulfilled rhetoric. We need elected officials who take oversized debt seriously enough to actually do something about it.
_John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission._

item.title: When unemployment becomes endless

According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, at least 1.8 million Americans have been actively looking for a fulltime job for more than 27 weeks. That’s over six months. In this episode, two people tell us what it’s like to navigate a never-ending job search. Plus: A surge in lone star ticks threatens the cattle industry, McDonald’s keeps huge amounts of data on frequent customers, and the national debt passes that $40 trillion threshold.

item.title: Tesla (TSLA) recalls over 2 million cars in China to add driver monitoring
item.description:
Tesla is recalling 2,740,642 vehicles in China to strengthen driver monitoring on its assisted-driving system, after regulators found that checking for a hand on the wheel isn’t enough to keep drivers watching the road.

The fix forces Tesla to use the car’s cabin camera to track the driver’s eyes — the same kind of monitoring Chinese drivers were recently caught defeating with $20 plastic doll heads.

Tesla is recalling 2,975,910 vehicles in China after the country’s market regulator determined that its emergency door release is too hard to find and operate in a crash.

It’s Tesla’s largest-ever recall in China, and it lands as the automaker’s door design faces mounting legal and regulatory pressure on two continents. Several other automakers who followed Tesla into similarly designed door releases have also issued similar recalls.

item.title: OpenAI to offer safety features for teens using ChatGPT
item.description:
OpenAI is launching ChatGPT for Teens, which has new guardrails to steer conversations from sensitive topics like self-harm or sexual content. It’ll also include parental controls and features intended to support studying without the cognitive offloading that often happens.


Plus, the surge in construction of AI data centers has increased the value of basically any component that goes into them. Now, thieves are increasingly targeting cargo shipments of materials bound for data centers. And Amazon is expanding its drone deliveries. Paresh Dave at Wired joins Marketplace’s Meghan McCarty Carino for these stories.


Everything we talked about:


“Introducing ChatGPT for Teens: Built for learning, backed by protections” from OpenAI


“OpenAI’s Second-Quarter Sales Show Tepid Growth Compared With Anthropic” from The Wall Street Journal


“States Seek $200 Billion From Meta Over Child Social Media Addiction Claims” from The New York Times


“‘The Worst I’ve Ever Seen’: Cargo Thefts Have Turned Violent in Pursuit of AI Hardware” from Wired


“Amazon Prime Air drone delivery is expanding to nearly 500 US cities and towns this year” from Amazon

item.title: If he wins the race, will Jackley be a rubber stamp for Trump?
item.description:
South Dakota has a number of important statewide election contests this fall. Our new Governor, Larry Rhoden, won a surprising landslide in the Republican runoff election over Toby Doeden, the extreme right-wing multimillionaire who had come in first in the primary but failed to clear the 35% threshold required for victory.

Rhoden faces Democrat Dan Ahlers, a seasoned former legislator and Democratic Party leader who lost the U.S. Senate race to Mike Rounds back in 2020.

Rounds, who has supported virtually all of Donald Trump's policies, is seeking a third term in the Senate, but his only opponent is Brian Bengs, running as an Independent, now that the Democratic nominee, Julian Beaudion, withdrew from the race at the last possible minute.

Bengs was the Democratic candidate for Senate against John Thune in 2022, shortly after he moved to South Dakota, and changed his voter registration back to Independent within weeks after his loss. Bengs likes to point out that he worked briefly as a ranger at Wind Cave National Park and is currently living in a camper while he builds a house to live in. 

Perhaps our most interesting statewide race is for U.S. Congress, since there is no incumbent running after Dusty Johnson finished a dismal third in the Republican primary for Governor. The Republicans nominated Marty Jackley, who has served as Attorney General and as U.S. Attorney over the years. Democrats are running Nikki Gronli, who made friends around the state when she served as our rural development director in the US Department of Agriculture, and has been campaigning tirelessly and holding town halls wherever people are willing to gather. 

"Nikki G for SD", who stands barely five feet tall, has put forth a program that includes fighting the fertilizer industry and meatpackers who are strangling our beleaguered family farmers, opposition to federal tax breaks for AI data centers, standing up to Donald Trump's tariffs on necessary farm inputs, as well as making Obamacare affordable for working families, improving health care on our reservations and working closely with tribal colleges, supporting early childhood education (Pre-K), and investing in rural schools and in the Disabilities Education Act.

You could say that Gronli does not want to leave any South Dakotan behind. Her positions are somewhat reminiscent of the last Democrat to represent this state in Washington, Senator Tim Johnson, who was never flashy but also never lost an election. 

For his part, Jackley has always been a competent attorney. He has managed to keep the Attorney General's office out of the headlines for most of his tenure.

It is interesting that Jackley would want to go to Washington at this point in his career. The overwhelming suspicion would be that Jackley will be yet another rubber stamp for Trump, supporting the directionless war against Iran and economic policies that favor billionaires and that prevent local communities from reining in (or even prohibiting) data centers in their midst.

If Jackley does not intend to serve as a Republican rubber stamp, he needs to explain convincingly where he will stand up for his constituents and eschew the party line. Otherwise, moderate Republican voters and many Independents may want to split their tickets and vote for Nikki Gronli. 

Jay Davis is a retired Rapid City attorney

The South Dakota Standard is offered freely and is supported by our readers. We have no political or commercial sponsorship. If you'd like to help us continue our mission to advance independent political and social commentary, you can do so by clicking on the "Donate" button that's on the sidebar to your right.
